[[File:WCDD Venn Diagram.png|thumb|upright=2|Venn Diagram showing the containment of weakly chained diagonally dominant (WCDD) matrices relative to weakly diagonally dominant (WDD) and strictly diagonally dominant (SDD) matrices.]]

In mathematics, the '''weakly chained diagonally dominant matrices''' are a family of [[nonsingular matrices]] that include the strictly [[diagonally dominant matrices]].

==Definition==

===Preliminaries===

We say row <math>i</math> of a complex matrix <math>A = (a_{ij})</math> is '''strictly diagonally dominant''' (SDD) if <math>|a_{ii}|>\textstyle{\sum_{j\neq i}}|a_{ij}|</math>. We say <math>A</math> is SDD if all of its rows are SDD. '''Weakly diagonally dominant''' (WDD) is defined with <math>\geq</math> instead.

The '''[[directed graph]]''' associated with an <math>m \times m</math> complex matrix <math>A = (a_{ij})</math> is given by the vertices <math>\{1, \ldots, m\}</math> and edges defined as follows: there exists an edge from <math>i \rightarrow j</math> if and only if <math>a_{ij} \neq 0</math>.

===Definition===

A complex square matrix <math>A</math> is said to be '''weakly chained diagonally dominant''' (WCDD) if
* <math>A</math> is WDD and
* for each row <math>i_1</math> that is ''not'' SDD, there exists a [[Walk (graph theory)|walk]] <math>i_1 \rightarrow i_2 \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow i_k</math> in the directed graph of <math>A</math> ending at an SDD row <math>i_k</math>.

==Example==

[[File:Graph of a WCDD matrix.png|thumb|upright=2|The directed graph associated with the WCDD matrix in the example. The first row, which is SDD, is highlighted. Note that regardless of which node <math>i</math> we start at, we can find a walk <math>i \rightarrow (i - 1) \rightarrow (i - 2) \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow 1</math>.]]
The <math>m \times m</math> matrix
:<math>\begin{pmatrix}1\\
-1 & 1\\
 & -1 & 1\\
 &  & \ddots & \ddots\\
 &  &  & -1 & 1
\end{pmatrix} </math>
is WCDD.

==Properties==

===Nonsingularity===

A WCDD matrix is nonsingular.<ref name="ShivakumarChew1974">{{cite journal|last1=Shivakumar|first1=P. N.|last2=Chew|first2=Kim Ho|title=A Sufficient Condition for Nonvanishing of Determinants|journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society|volume=43|issue=1|year=1974|pages=63|issn=0002-9939|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1974-0332820-0|url=http://www.ams.org/journals/proc/1974-043-01/S0002-9939-1974-0332820-0/S0002-9939-1974-0332820-0.pdf|doi-access=free}}</ref>

''Proof'':<ref name="AzimzadehForsyth2016">{{cite journal|last1=Azimzadeh|first1=Parsiad|last2=Forsyth|first2=Peter A.|title=Weakly Chained Matrices, Policy Iteration, and Impulse Control|journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis|volume=54|issue=3|year=2016|pages=1341–1364|issn=0036-1429|doi=10.1137/15M1043431|arxiv=1510.03928|s2cid=29143430 }}</ref>
Let <math>A=(a_{ij})</math> be a WCDD matrix. Suppose there exists a nonzero <math>x</math> in the [[Kernel (linear algebra)|null space]] of <math>A</math>.
[[Without loss of generality]], let <math>i_1</math> be such that <math>|x_{i_1}|=1\geq|x_j|</math> for all <math>j</math>.
Since <math>A</math> is WCDD, we may pick a walk <math>i_1\rightarrow i_2\rightarrow\cdots\rightarrow i_k</math> ending at an SDD row <math>i_k</math>.

Taking moduli on both sides of
:<math>-a_{i_1 i_1}x_{i_1} = \sum_{j\neq i_1} a_{i_{1} j}x_j</math>
and applying the [[triangle inequality]] yields
:<math>\left|a_{i_1 i_1}\right|\leq\sum_{j\neq i_1}\left|a_{i_1 j}\right|\left|x_j\right|\leq\sum_{j\neq i_1}\left|a_{i_1 j}\right|,</math>
and hence row <math>i_1</math> is not SDD.
Moreover, since <math>A</math> is WDD, the above chain of inequalities holds with equality so that <math>|x_{j}|=1</math> whenever <math>a_{i_1 j}\neq0</math>.
Therefore, <math>|x_{i_2}|=1</math>.
Repeating this argument with <math>i_2</math>, <math>i_3</math>, etc., we find that <math>i_k</math> is not SDD, a contradiction. <math>\square</math>

Recalling that an [[Irreducibility (mathematics)|irreducible]] matrix is one whose associated directed graph is [[strongly connected]], a trivial corollary of the above is that an ''irreducibly diagonally dominant matrix'' (i.e., an irreducible WDD matrix with at least one SDD row) is nonsingular.<ref name="HornJohnson1990">{{cite book|last1=Horn|first1=Roger A.|last2=Johnson|first2=Charles R.|title=Matrix analysis|year=1990|publisher=Cambridge University Press, Cambridge}}</ref>

===Relationship with nonsingular M-matrices===

The following are equivalent:<ref name="Azimzadeh2017">{{cite journal|last1=Azimzadeh|first1=Parsiad|title=A fast and stable test to check if a weakly diagonally dominant matrix is a nonsingular M-Matrix|journal=Mathematics of Computation|year=2019|volume=88|issue=316|pages=783–800|doi=10.1090/mcom/3347|arxiv=1701.06951|bibcode=2017arXiv170106951A|s2cid=3356041 }}</ref>
* <math>A</math> is a nonsingular WDD [[M-matrix]].
* <math>A</math> is a nonsingular WDD [[L-matrix]];
* <math>A</math> is a WCDD [[L-matrix]];

In fact, WCDD L-matrices were studied (by [[James H. Bramble]] and B. E. Hubbard) as early as 1964 in a journal article<ref name="BrambleHubbard1964">{{cite journal|last1=Bramble|first1=James H.|last2=Hubbard|first2=B. E.|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics|volume=43|year=1964|pages=117–132|title=On a finite difference analogue of an elliptic problem which is neither diagonally dominant nor of non-negative type|doi=10.1002/sapm1964431117}}</ref> in which they appear under the alternate name of ''matrices of positive type''.

Moreover, if <math>A</math> is an <math>n\times n</math> WCDD L-matrix, we can bound its inverse as follows:<ref name="ShivakumarWilliams1996">{{cite journal|last1=Shivakumar|first1=P. N.|last2=Williams|first2=Joseph J.|last3=Ye|first3=Qiang|last4=Marinov|first4=Corneliu A.|title=On Two-Sided Bounds Related to Weakly Diagonally Dominant M-Matrices with Application to Digital Circuit Dynamics|journal=SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications|volume=17|issue=2|year=1996|pages=298–312|issn=0895-4798|doi=10.1137/S0895479894276370}}</ref>
:<math>\left\Vert A^{-1}\right\Vert _{\infty}\leq\sum_{i}\left[a_{ii}\prod_{j=1}^{i}(1-u_{j})\right]^{-1}</math> &nbsp; where &nbsp; <math>u_{i}=\frac{1}{\left|a_{ii}\right|}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}\left|a_{ij}\right|.</math>
Note that <math>u_n</math> is always zero and that the right-hand side of the bound above is <math>\infty</math> whenever one or more of the constants <math>u_i</math> is one.

Tighter bounds for the inverse of a WCDD L-matrix are known.<ref name="ChengHuang2007">{{cite journal|last1=Cheng|first1=Guang-Hui|last2=Huang|first2=Ting-Zhu|title=An upper bound for <math>\Vert A^{-1}\Vert _{\infty}</math> of strictly diagonally dominant M-matrices|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=426|issue=2–3|year=2007|pages=667–673|issn=0024-3795|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2007.06.001|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Li2008">{{cite journal|last1=Li|first1=Wen|title=The infinity norm bound for the inverse of nonsingular diagonal dominant matrices|journal=Applied Mathematics Letters|volume=21|issue=3|year=2008|pages=258–263|issn=0893-9659|doi=10.1016/j.aml.2007.03.018|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Wang2009">{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Ping|title=An upper bound for <math>\Vert A^{-1}\Vert _{\infty}</math> of strictly diagonally dominant M-matrices|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=431|issue=5–7|year=2009|pages=511–517|issn=0024-3795|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2009.02.037|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="HuangZhu2010">{{cite journal|last1=Huang|first1=Ting-Zhu|last2=Zhu|first2=Yan|title=Estimation of <math>\Vert A^{-1}\Vert _{\infty}</math> for weakly chained diagonally dominant M-matrices|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|volume=432|issue=2–3|year=2010|pages=670–677|issn=0024-3795|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2009.09.012|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Applications==

Due to their relationship with [[M-matrix|M-matrices]] (see [[#Relationship_with_M-matrices|above]]), WCDD matrices appear often in practical applications.
An example is given below.

===Monotone numerical schemes===

WCDD L-matrices arise naturally from monotone approximation schemes for [[partial differential equations]].

For example, consider the one-dimensional [[Poisson problem]]
:<math>u^{\prime \prime}(x) + g(x)= 0</math> &nbsp; for &nbsp; <math>x \in (0,1)</math>
with [[Dirichlet boundary conditions]] <math>u(0)=u(1)=0</math>.
Letting <math>\{0,h,2h,\ldots,1\}</math> be a numerical grid (for some positive <math>h</math> that divides unity), a monotone finite difference scheme for the Poisson problem takes the form of 
:<math>-\frac{1}{h^2}A\vec{u} + \vec{g} = 0</math> &nbsp; where &nbsp; <math>[\vec{g}]_j = g(jh)</math>
and
:<math>A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\
-1 & 2 & -1\\
 & -1 & 2 & -1\\
 &  & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots\\
 &  &  & -1 & 2 & -1\\
 &  &  &  & -1 & 2
\end{pmatrix}.</math>
Note that <math>A</math> is a WCDD L-matrix.
